                                    <div class="single-heading">
                                        <h2> 25.1 Purpose of procurement and contract management</h2>
                                    </div>
                                                                        <div class="single-content mt-1 full-width">
                                        <p>The purpose of procurement and contract management, in project delivery, is to ensure that the products and services bought as part of resourcing the work or developing the outputs represent value for money and can be delivered within an acceptable level of risk.</p>
                                    </div>
                                     

                                    
                            </div>
                            
                            <div id="section-2" class="single-section highlight">

                                    <div class="single-heading">
                                        <h2> 25.2 Key points</h2>
                                    </div>
                                                                        <div class="single-content mt-1 full-width">
                                        <ul>
<li>Procurement and contract management must secure value for money when buying goods, works and services, in compliance with the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/government-functional-standard-govs-008-commercial-and-commercial-continuous-improvement-assessment-framework" class="link" ><em>Government Functional Standard for Commercial</em></a> and the relevant <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/procurement-policy-notes" class="link" ><em>Procurement policy notes</em></a>.</li>
<li>Conduct commercial activities in accordance with relevant <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ppn-0623-the-commercial-playbooks/procurement-policy-note-the-commercial-playbooks-html" class="link" ><em>Commercial playbooks</em></a> and the organisation’s governance and management framework.</li>
<li>Identify procurement needs early, appoint commercial specialists, and engage with the supply market in time for suppliers to understand the requirements and prepare competitive offers.</li>
<li>Manage contract performance through proportionate key performance indicators, and ensure reporting is accurate and timely.</li>
<li>Raise risks and issues early with the senior responsible owner, commercial specialists and any other relevant stakeholders so that under-performance can be managed and disputes resolved.</li>
</ul>
                                    </div>
                                     

                                    
                            </div>
                            
                            <div id="section-3" class="single-section ">

                                    <div class="single-heading">
                                        <h2> 25.3 Why procure and manage contracts?</h2>
                                    </div>
                                                                        <div class="single-content mt-1 full-width">
                                        <p>Government portfolios, programmes and projects are wide-ranging, delivering infrastructure through to the complex software, responding to humanitarian crises and transforming public services.</p>
<p>It is not possible or desirable for government organisations to maintain the permanent capability and capacity needed to deliver all this work. Procurement is the right approach when the supply market is better placed to provide the goods, works or services needed, helping achieve better value for money and mitigating risk through external support.</p>
<p>Once contracts are awarded, managing them effectively is what ensures suppliers deliver the intended deliverables, outputs and outcomes.</p>
                                    </div>
                                     

                                    
                            </div>
                            
                            <div id="section-4" class="single-section ">

                                    <div class="single-heading">
                                        <h2> 25.4 What is procurement and contract management?</h2>
                                    </div>
                                                                        <div class="single-content mt-1 full-width">
                                        <p>Procurement and contract management are the activities that enable the portfolio, programme or project manager to secure value for money when buying goods, works and services in the delivery of government policy.</p>
<p>Procurement and contract management activities include:</p>
<ul>
<li>defining the requirements to meet the needs of the portfolio, programme or project</li>
<li>procuring those goods, works and services from the supply market</li>
<li>managing the subsequent contracts and suppliers to maximise benefits to the organisation</li>
</ul>
<p>Where a solution is primarily delivered through a single procurement, these activities align to the reference project life cycle from the <a href="https://projectdelivery.gov.uk/library-product/government-functional-standard-govs-002-project-delivery/" class="link" ><em>Government Functional Standard for Project Delivery</em></a> (see Figure 25.1) with:</p>
<ul>
<li>definition work, resulting in a route to market being selected, being undertaken across the feasibility and appraisal stages</li>
<li>procurement work, including invitation to tender and selecting the preferred supplier, being undertaken during the definition stage</li>
<li>award of the contract and its management being undertaken across the delivery and operations stages</li>
</ul>
                                    </div>
                                     

                                    
                            </div>

                                        <h2>  </h2>
                                    </div>
                                                                        <div class="single-content mt-1 ">
                                        <p>Programmes and projects might also have a number of procurements and contracts throughout the life cycle, providing different resources and developing different outputs that all contribute to the overall outcome.</p>
<p>Procurement and contract management must conform with the <em><a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/commercial-operating-standards-for-government" class="link" title="Government Functional Standard for Commercial">Government Functional Standard for Commercial</a></em>.</p>
                                    </div>
                                     

                                    
                            </div>
                            
                            <div id="section-5" class="single-section ">

                                    <div class="single-heading">
                                        <h2> 25.5 Who procures and manages contracts?</h2>
                                    </div>
                                     

                                    
                            </div>
                            
                            <div id="section-6" class="single-section ">

                                    <div class="single-heading">
                                        <h3> 25.5.1 Overview</h3>
                                    </div>
                                                                        <div class="single-content mt-1 full-width">
                                        <p>Everyone working in government project delivery has a responsibility to ensure that public resources are managed and used efficiently, effectively and in line with legal requirements, government policy and standards. This includes the need to procure services and work in a way which is transparent, meets requirements and is value for money.</p>
<p>Most project delivery requires the involvement of qualified commercial professionals. These could be working within the immediate team, sponsoring organisation or other organisations, such as the Government Commercial Function, or public buying organisations.</p>
<p>Accountability and responsibility for commercial management should be defined within the governance and management framework and reviewed on a regular basis.</p>
<p>It is important to understand how commercial roles work in relation to project delivery in government. The key roles are set out below, with more information available in the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/commercial-operating-standards-for-government" class="link" ><em>Government Functional Standard for Commercial</em></a> and in the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/government-commercial-function-people-standards-for-the-profession" class="link" ><em>People standards for the commercial profession</em></a>.</p>
                                    </div>
                                     

                                    
                            </div>
                            
                            <div id="section-7" class="single-section ">

                                    <div class="single-heading">
                                        <h3> 25.5.2 Commercial roles in government</h3>
                                    </div>
                                                                        <div class="single-content mt-1 full-width">
                                        <p>Commercial management in government takes place within a formal framework of accountabilities set out in the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/commercial-operating-standards-for-government" class="link" ><em>Government Functional Standard for Commercial</em></a>.</p>
<p><strong>Commercial directors</strong> and their teams work to the commercial strategy agreed for their department, supported by a number of central government commercial teams. Their activities are co-ordinated by the Government Chief Commercial Officer.</p>
<p>These central commercial teams offer specialist support for departments:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>complex transactions</strong> supports departments with complex procurements, negotiations with suppliers and on all cross-government disputes</li>
<li><strong>markets and suppliers</strong> provides supplier, market and sector intelligence to departments</li>
<li><strong>commercial continuous improvements</strong> offers guidance, support, standards and controls on good commercial practice</li>
<li><strong>commercial capability</strong> is a programme set up to develop the commercial capability of colleagues across government</li>
</ul>
                                    </div>
                                     

                                    
                            </div>
                            
                            <div id="section-8" class="single-section ">

                                    <div class="single-heading">
                                        <h3> 25.5.3 Commercial roles in project delivery</h3>
                                    </div>
                                                                        <div class="single-content mt-1 full-width">
                                        <p>The <strong>portfolio director</strong>, in a portfolio, or <strong>senior responsible owner</strong>, in a programme or project, is accountable for ensuring effective commercial management, including owning the commercial management framework and plan. They ensure work is undertaken to determine if there is a need to procure services and work from the supply chain.</p>
<p>The <strong>portfolio, programme or project manager</strong>, as appropriate, is accountable for ensuring development and implementation of the commercial management framework and commercial plan, and ongoing commercial control, reporting and accounting activities. This work is normally led by a professionally qualified <strong>commercial practitioner</strong>, <strong>lead or specialist</strong> and supported by a commercial team, usually based within a support office.</p>
<p>Once the commercial agreement has been signed, the contract is managed by a <strong>contract manager</strong>. A contract manager should ideally be involved during the procurement. Who fulfils this role will depend on the nature or complexity of the contract. For example, the role of contract manager could be fulfilled by a <strong>work package manager</strong> or, for complex contracts, could be fulfilled by a <strong>commercial practitioner</strong>.</p>
<p>More detail on professional commercial roles is set out in the Government Commercial Function’s <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/government-commercial-function-people-standards-for-the-profession" class="link" ><em>People standards for the commercial profession</em></a>.</p>
                                    </div>
                                     

                                    
                            </div>
                            
                            <div id="section-9" class="single-section ">

                                    <div class="single-heading">
                                        <h2> 25.6 How to procure and manage contracts</h2>
                                    </div>
                                     

                                    
                            </div>
                            
                            <div id="section-10" class="single-section ">

                                    <div class="single-heading">
                                        <h3> 25.6.1 What to consider when procuring and managing contracts</h3>
                                    </div>
                                     

                                    
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.1.1                                                     Complying with the Procurement Act 2023</h4>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>The <a href="https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2023/54/contents" class="link" ><em>Procurement Act 2023</em></a> (and relevant regulations made under the Act) applies to contracting authorities in England, Wales and Northern Ireland and to contracting authorities with reserved functions carrying out procurement in Scotland. See <em><a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/procurement-act-2023-guidance-documents-plan-phase" class="link" title="Guidance: Contracting authority definition">Guidance: Contracting authority definition</a> </em>and<em> <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/procurement-act-2023-guidance-documents-plan-phase" class="link" title="Guidance: Devolved contracting authorities">Guidance: Devolved contracting authorities</a>.</em></p>
<p>Some devolved Welsh and transferred Northern Ireland procurements are exempt from a small number of requirements of the <a href="https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2023/54/contents" class="link" ><em>Procurement Act 2023</em></a>. These exemptions can be found in the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/tpp-knowledge-drop-supporting-factsheets" class="link" ><em>Procurement Act 2023 knowledge drop for contracting authorities: Wales</em></a> and <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/tpp-knowledge-drop-supporting-factsheets" class="link" ><em>Procurement Act 2023 knowledge drop for contracting authorities: Northern Ireland</em></a>. Scotland maintains its own procurement legislation which also applies to devolved Scottish authorities.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h5> Which contracts are covered?</h5>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>Generally, the provisions in the <a href="https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2023/54/contents" class="link" ><em>Procurement Act 2023</em></a> must be applied to a ‘covered procurement’. A covered procurement is the award, entry into and management of a public contract. A public contract is a contract of a particular type that is above the relevant threshold (for goods, services and works) and which is not an exempted contract.</p>
<p>However, some rules in the <a href="https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2023/54/contents" class="link" ><em>Procurement Act 2023</em> </a>must be applied to procurements not caught by the definition of ‘covered procurement’ and that is why there is a wider definition of ‘procurement’ (the award, entry into and management of a contract), which means any procurement. This allows some limited rules for contracts not caught under the definition of ‘covered procurement’, such as below-threshold procurements; this is to ensure certain treaty obligations are complied with.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h5> How to stay compliant</h5>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>Contracting authorities should ensure they are familiar with the obligations set out in the <a href="https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2023/54/contents" class="link" ><em>Procurement Act 2023</em></a> as soon as they become aware they have to carry out a procurement. For example, this would include informative processes like pre-market engagement where they would need to have regard to the procurement objectives in choosing how and who to engage with. Also, when drafting the contract scope, award criteria and KPIs, consideration needs to be given to things like the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-procurement-policy-statement" class="link" ><em>National procurement policy statement</em></a> or the <a href="https://www.gov.wales/procurement-policy-statement-html" class="link" ><em>Wales procurement policy statement</em></a>. <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/procurement-act-2023-guidance-documents" class="link" ><em>Procurement Act 2023 guidance documents collection</em></a> can help.</p>
<p>Portfolio, programme and project teams should continue to engage with professionally qualified commercial practitioners, leads or specialists from their organisation’s commercial team as soon as the potential need to procure has been identified. This will help to ensure that the requirements of the <a href="https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2023/54/contents" class="link" ><em>Procurement Act 2023</em></a>, as well as other regulations, policies and procedures, are taken into account at the earliest opportunity.</p>
<p>Those with accountability for the appropriate procurement and management of contracts, such as portfolio directors and senior responsible owners should make themselves familiar with <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/procurement-act-2023-short-guides/the-procurement-act-2023-a-short-guide-for-senior-leaders-html" class="link" ><em>The Procurement Act 2023: A short guide for senior leaders</em></a>. Members of portfolio, programme or project teams who are not commercial practitioners but have regular interactions with procurement should make themselves familiar with <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/the-official-transforming-public-procurement-knowledge-drops" class="link" ><em>The official transforming public procurement knowledge drops</em></a> and the supporting <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/tpp-knowledge-drop-supporting-factsheets" class="link" ><em>TPP knowledge drop supporting factsheets</em></a>.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.1.2                                                     Ensuring consistency with organisational systems and processes</h4>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>Procurement and contract management needs to integrate with the wider commercial management arrangements in the sponsoring organisation within which it sits. This is particularly the case at portfolio level, where a portfolio can cover the whole of an organisation’s procurement activities and associated investment and resource spend.</p>
<p>Commercial management arrangements should be consistent with the sponsoring organisation’s processes and use their commercial management and accounting systems wherever possible. The commercial processes should be designed and operated to ensure consistency with the organisational commercial hierarchy and in capturing data across the organisation’s portfolios, programmes and projects.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.1.3                                                     Complying with procurement policy</h4>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>Government Commercial Agency publishes the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/public-sector-procurement-policy" class="link" ><em>Public procurement policy</em></a> which sets out the directives, regulations, policies and guidance relating to the procurement of supplies, services and works for the public sector.</p>
<p>The commercial policies reflecting the government’s priorities are set out in <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/procurement-policy-notes" class="link" ><em>Procurement policy notes</em></a> and come with supporting guidance for implementation. <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/procurement-policy-notes" class="link" ><em>Procurement policy notes</em></a> detail the actions to be taken by contracting authorities when undertaking public sector procurement and so are implemented into the parent organisation’s commercial management arrangements. An example of a note is <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ppn-002-taking-account-of-social-value-in-the-award-of-contracts" class="link" ><em>PPN 002: Taking account of social value in the award of contracts</em></a>, which supports compliance with the <em><a href="https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2012/3" class="link" title="Public Services (Social Value) Act">Public Services (Social Value) Act</a></em><a href="https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2012/3" class="link" title=" 2012"> 2012</a>. See <a href="https://projectdelivery.gov.uk/teal-book/home/part-e-planning-and-control/chapter-19-benefits-management/#section-9" class="link" title="19.6.3.5 on its role in supporting identifying and categorising a benefit">19.6.3.5 on its role in supporting identifying and categorising a benefit</a>.</p>
<p>The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs also publishes mandatory <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/sustainable-procurement-the-government-buying-standards-gbs" class="link" ><em>Government Buying Standards</em></a> for buying goods and services to support procurement of more sustainable and efficient products and engage with your suppliers to understand and reduce the impacts of their supply chains.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.1.4                                                     Working with suppliers and accessing the market</h4>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>Commercial relationships with third-party suppliers can vary depending on the complexity and duration of the relationship. Project delivery teams, working with commercial specialists, should develop an understanding of how best to work with and access the market and suppliers.</p>
<p>Simple transactional commercial relationships might be suitable when the requirements are well understood and with limited risks. In these circumstances, it is often possible to procure from a pre-existing framework, catalogue or dynamic purchasing system, often administered by public buying organisations, such as:</p>
<ul>
<li>frameworks are available to public sector organisations to procure goods, works and services with pre-determined terms, conditions and prices</li>
<li>catalogues contain a pre-determined list of typically low-cost items that can be purchased with limited commercial specialist input</li>
<li>dynamic purchasing systems are similar to frameworks, but the list of available suppliers changes</li>
</ul>
<p>For complex or high-risk requirements, it is necessary to establish a bespoke contract, through an open competition, with a third-party supplier or suppliers. The attributes of complex requirements in the context of procurement and contracts include:</p>
<ul>
<li>first generation outsourcing</li>
<li>significant transformation of service delivery obtaining services with limited competition or where government is the only customer</li>
<li>any service obtained by a contract that is considered novel or contentious</li>
</ul>
<p>Advice should be sought from commercial specialists where a procurement involves complex or high-risk requirements to understand how the market should be engaged and how to approach the procurement.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.1.5                                                     Assuring commercial activities</h4>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>Project delivery teams should have a defined and established approach to commercial assurance which is integrated into the wider assurance and approvals framework for the portfolio, programme or project. Assurance activities focused on commercial activities and decisions should be proportionate to the complexity, risk and value of the procurement and contract.</p>
<p>In relation to the assurance of commercial activities, consideration should be given to:</p>
<ul>
<li>industry security so as to protect government from threats related to suppliers having access to classified, or vulnerable to compromise, information, assets and estates</li>
<li>commercial spend controls which, when applicable, should involve consulting with the Cabinet Office and HM Treasury to facilitate commercial assurance activity and ministerial approvals</li>
<li>counter fraud and serious and organised economic crime, both of which are a significant risk to the UK public sector, have far-reaching financial and reputational consequences and can pose a national security issue</li>
</ul>
<p>Where relevant, commercial assurance activities should also be undertaken in accordance with the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/government-functional-standard-govs-007-security" class="link" ><em>Government Functional Standard for Security</em></a> and the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/government-functional-standard-govs-013-counter-fraud" class="link" ><em>Government Functional Standard for Counter Fraud</em></a>.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.1.6                                                     Dealing with complex services and high-risk procurements</h4>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>When a complex service is outsourced for the first time and there is limited information available about the requirements and risks, a pilot should be run as part of a programme or project to test viability and make any necessary changes. Options for running pilots include:</p>
<ul>
<li>trials and proofs of concept</li>
<li>identifying potential innovations</li>
<li>identifying lessons learned</li>
</ul>
<p>Where the contract is high-risk (for example, complex requirements, unproven market capability, uncertain policy environment), methods such as ‘should cost’ modelling should be used to assess the risks relating to different offers. Such contracts usually require a bespoke procurement approach that allows for project delivery teams to obtain targeted responses from the supply market that meet the business needs.</p>
<p>Counter fraud risk assessments should be used when selecting suppliers for complex contracts and after the award of the contract to ensure payments are made in line with the agreed contractual terms.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.1.7                                                     Understanding how the contract is to be managed</h4>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>When services, works or goods are being procured, how the contract is to be managed should be considered. The <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-contract-management-playbook" class="link" ><em>Contract management playbook </em></a>sets out principles. This includes involving the intended contract manager during the procurement and ensuring that they have reviewed and understood aspects such as:</p>
<ul>
<li>the scope of the work, including contract management resource implications, statutory obligations, the obligations of both parties and provisions for intellectual property rights or commercial exploitation levy</li>
<li>the payment regime, including what is covered by fixed and variable or call-off costs and how these will be calculated, budget controls, pricing provisions for future change control and any implication these might have on the resources needed to manage the contract</li>
<li>the key performance indicators, including the frequency and ease of data collection, validation and reporting requirements (see <a href="https://projectdelivery.gov.uk/teal-book/the-teal-book/part-e-planning-and-control/chapter-18-reporting/" class="link" title="Chapter 18: Reporting">Chapter 18: Reporting</a>)</li>
<li>the provisions for managing under-performance and breach of contract, including dispute resolution, arbitration and step-in rights</li>
<li>the provisions for changes to the contract (variations), including ensuring that any changes are justified and controlled (see <a href="https://projectdelivery.gov.uk/teal-book/the-teal-book/part-e-planning-and-control/chapter-22-change-control/" class="link" title="Chapter 22: Change control">Chapter 22: Change control</a>)</li>
<li>the provisions for risk management, in accordance with the risk management approach for the portfolio, programme or project overall and considering the need for agreed resolution plans to ensure continuity of service (see <a href="https://projectdelivery.gov.uk/teal-book/the-teal-book/part-e-planning-and-control/chapter-20-risk-management/" class="link" title="Chapter 20: Risk management">Chapter 20: Risk management</a> and <a href="https://projectdelivery.gov.uk/teal-book/the-teal-book/part-e-planning-and-control/chapter-21-issue-management/" class="link" title="Chapter 21: Issue management">Chapter 21: Issue management</a>)</li>
<li>the exit provisions, including break clauses and notice periods, the triggers for termination, supplier and client obligations in relation to exit and transition. Those who will be involved in managing the contract should be involved throughout the procurement to ensure that they are able to build relationships with the eventual supplier and wider market and so that the contract that is awarded can be operated and administered</li>
</ul>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.1.8                                                     Developing strong working relationships</h4>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>Strong internal and external working relationships help to facilitate the delivery and management of a contract. This can be achieved by a shared understanding of the role of the contract manager and the roles and responsibilities on the supplier side. Documenting these respective responsibilities, and behaviours, in a joint document, such as a contract management plan or charter, can help, especially if there is ever a change in the people involved.</p>
<p>How the contract manager and supplier communicate should be considered and planned for. This includes both regular structured and informal communication routes which are open and easily used as well as routes for formal notices.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                            </div>
                            
                            <div id="section-11" class="single-section ">

                                    <div class="single-heading">
                                        <h3> 25.6.2 Preparing to procure and manage contracts</h3>
                                    </div>
                                     

                                    
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.2.1                                                     Overview</h4>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>Preparing for commercial management is important, to ensure that the commercial management framework put in place meets the requirements in the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/commercial-operating-standards-for-government" class="link" ><em>Government Functional Standard for Commercial</em></a>, the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/procurement-act-2023-guidance-documents" class="link" ><em>Procurement Act 2023</em></a> (see 25.6.1.1 on complying with the Act), any relevant <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/public-sector-procurement-policy" class="link" ><em>Public p</em><em>rocurement policy</em></a> and organisational practices. In particular, there needs to be a clearly defined mandate and objectives for the work, as these will determine the nature of the commercial activities and resources involved and how these might need to be managed.</p>
<p>In a portfolio, for example, commercial management is closely linked to wider organisational commercial practices. Where a new portfolio is being established or arrangements are being reshaped, particularly at organisational level, strategic decisions might be needed from the accounting officer and executive board on how portfolio commercial activity is to be planned and managed.</p>
<p>Commercial management in programmes and projects normally operates within existing commercial management arrangements. Defining the commercial governance and management framework for the work is a critical early task, starting as soon as any need to source goods or services from a third-party has been identified. This helps ensure that commercial activities can be planned and costs can be budgeted for. Where necessary, an initial framework can be put in place and then developed as the work expands and commercial planning and management requirements increase.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.2.2                                                     Define the commercial management framework</h4>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>The governance and management framework for commercial forms part of the overall governance and management framework for the work and should be integrated with the framework in place for the organisation.</p>
<p>The first step is to take a strategic view of likely requirements for commercial management. The commercial needs in project delivery can vary widely, from the outsourcing of the design, development and delivery of the solution, short term needs for professional services and goods through to commercial pipeline and market development activities. Depending on the likely commercial needs of a programme or project, <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/cabinet-office-controls" class="link" ><em>Cabinet Office controls</em></a> and the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/treasury-approvals-process-for-programmes-and-projects" class="link" ><em>Treasury approvals process for projects and programmes</em></a> might apply.</p>
<p>This initial view should provide a basis for defining the core elements of the framework. This should cover key requirements and controls, for example:</p>
<ul>
<li>core standards and government requirements to be followed</li>
<li>the criteria for the tiering and segmentation of commercial agreements and suppliers</li>
<li>authority limits and decision-making roles and rules</li>
<li>degree of autonomy</li>
<li>assurance needs</li>
<li>reporting structure</li>
<li>accountabilities and responsibilities for undertaking commercial practices</li>
</ul>
<p>In a portfolio, the framework sets the parameters for managing commercial activities at portfolio level, as well as what is expected of programmes and projects within the portfolio, in line with the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/commercial-operating-standards-for-government" class="link" ><em>Government Functional Standard for Commercial </em></a> and <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/project-delivery-functional-standard" class="link" ><em>Government Functional Standard </em><em>for Project Delivery</em></a>. How this works depends on whether commercial management activities are undertaken through the portfolio, or separately. Even in the latter case, there should be full visibility of programme and project commercial needs and activities at portfolio level, as this is essential for accurate portfolio monitoring, reporting and intervention. Consideration should be given to whether a commercial pipeline, which feeds into the organisation’s commercial pipeline and might contribute to a published commercial projection, is needed. The portfolio commercial management framework should set out how this works.</p>
<p>For organisational portfolios, the framework should be approved by the chief commercial officer and accounting officer and the appropriate governance board, usually the organisational portfolio board or investment committee. Below this level, the framework should be approved by the portfolio director.</p>
<p>In a programme or project, the oversight of procurement and contract management should be delegated to the senior responsible owner to manage as a core element of their accountability for the work. The senior responsible owner can make further sub-delegations, normally to the programme or project manager, so they can manage commercial activities on a day-to-day basis, and sometimes beyond. The framework plays an important part in demonstrating how the senior responsible owner plans to exercise their commercial responsibilities in line with their delegated authority (and taking account of any sub-delegations), to meet the required standards and maintain commercial discipline in line with organisational and portfolio requirements. At programme and project level, the framework should be approved by the senior responsible owner and the appropriate governance board.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.2.3                                                     Identify the appropriate systems, processes and tools</h4>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>The platforms, applications, processes and tools needed to support commercial planning, procurement and control should be identified early. This usually means using existing organisational commercial and reporting platforms and established processes, but might need also to be supplemented by additional processes or specialist tools.</p>
<p>For smaller initiatives, commercial data, modelling and analysis is often handled on spreadsheets. Some organisations provide specialised tools for managing commercial activities which interface with their existing platforms, and these can save considerable time and effort on rekeying or uploading data, particularly at portfolio level but also for programme and project managers in reporting upwards. For larger and more complex endeavours, specialised planning and control software, incorporating commercial data, can be used: see <a href="https://projectdelivery.gov.uk/teal-book/the-teal-book/part-e-planning-and-control/chapter-16-planning/" class="link" title="Chapter 16: Planning">Chapter 16: Planning</a>.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.2.4                                                     Brief the team on the contracts</h4>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>Team members who interact or work with a supplier need to understand the contract and what its terms mean for their own responsibilities. Contracts include obligations on both parties which, if not respected, can lead to a material breach of contract.</p>
<p>Team members should understand:</p>
<ul>
<li>how these obligations are reflected in the contract management plan</li>
<li>what authority they have as individuals</li>
<li>what they are and are not allowed to agree, approve or instruct, so they do not inadvertently compromise the contract</li>
</ul>
<p>Contracts also include strict timescales and specify a route and named person for formal contract notices. It is the responsibility of the sender to make sure communications are received, not the receiving party.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                            </div>
