                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.3.2                                                     Develop and maintain the procurement management framework</h4>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>The approach to procurement and contract management should be defined including any processes, methods, tools and techniques to be used. This forms part of the overall governance and management framework for the work (see <a href="https://projectdelivery.gov.uk/teal-book/the-teal-book/part-a-project-delivery-in-government/chapter-4-governance-and-management/" class="link" title="Chapter 4: Governance and management">Chapter 4: Governance and management</a> and 25.6.2.2 on defining the commercial management framework).</p>
<p>Commercial management in project delivery is governed by the overall government control framework in <a href="https://projectdelivery.gov.uk/library-product/managing-public-money/" class="link restricted" ><em>Managing public money</em><span class='show-for-sr'> (requires sign in)</span><svg width="18" role="img" aria-hidden="true" height="18" viewBox="0 0 18 18" tabindex="-1" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M6.2921 5.9375V7.625H11.7056V5.9375C11.7056 4.38359 10.4944 3.125 8.99887 3.125C7.50338 3.125 6.2921 4.38359 6.2921 5.9375ZM4.12669 7.625V5.9375C4.12669 3.14258 6.30902 0.875 8.99887 0.875C11.6887 0.875 13.871 3.14258 13.871 5.9375V7.625H14.4124C15.6068 7.625 16.5778 8.63398 16.5778 9.875V16.625C16.5778 17.866 15.6068 18.875 14.4124 18.875H3.58534C2.39097 18.875 1.41992 17.866 1.41992 16.625V9.875C1.41992 8.63398 2.39097 7.625 3.58534 7.625H4.12669Z" fill="#0B0C0C"/></svg></a>, and how that is then applied within the organisation in which it takes place. It is important, nonetheless, to set out the specific commercial management controls required within the portfolio, programme or project, aligned to the scale, complexity and risk profile of the work. It is also important to monitor the operation of the framework to ensure that it remains effective and appropriate as the work proceeds, particularly if things change. If necessary, it should be updated.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.3.3                                                     Define the procurement</h4>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h5> Overview</h5>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>Defining a procurement involves:</p>
<ul>
<li>shaping business needs and the delivery model assessment</li>
<li>supply market analysis and early engagement</li>
<li>analysis of commercial options</li>
<li>setting criteria for selecting suppliers</li>
</ul>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h5> Shaping business needs and the delivery model assessment</h5>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>Options for commercial delivery should be evaluated at the outset of a new programme or project to inform the business need and provide sufficient time to select the commercial delivery model to be used.</p>
<p>An assessment of the delivery model should be undertaken to provide an analytical, evidence-based recommendation on whether a programme or project team should deliver a service or part of a service in-house, procure from the market or adopt a hybrid solution. Assessments should be proportionate to the scale and complexity of the work.</p>
<p>Commercial specialists should be appointed early to support definition of the business need and oversee the project delivery commercial activities and delivery model assessment.</p>
<p>Business needs should be translated into commercial requirements which can be defined in a contract or equivalent commercial format. Commercial requirements should be accessible to the supply market, be sufficiently flexible to allow for potential future changes or innovation and enable performance and outcomes to be measured.</p>
<p>Particular care should be given to the need to protect against the risk of fraud, bribery and corruption. There are clear rules and duties of due diligence which should be adhered to when awarding purchasing contracts or grants. This should be considered at an early stage, and the design of the proposal should consider proportionate counter measures. More detail can be found in the <a href="https://projectdelivery.gov.uk/library-product/the-green-book-and-accompanying-guidance-and-documents/" class="link restricted" ><em>Green Book</em><span class='show-for-sr'> (requires sign in)</span><svg width="18" role="img" aria-hidden="true" height="18" viewBox="0 0 18 18" tabindex="-1" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M6.2921 5.9375V7.625H11.7056V5.9375C11.7056 4.38359 10.4944 3.125 8.99887 3.125C7.50338 3.125 6.2921 4.38359 6.2921 5.9375ZM4.12669 7.625V5.9375C4.12669 3.14258 6.30902 0.875 8.99887 0.875C11.6887 0.875 13.871 3.14258 13.871 5.9375V7.625H14.4124C15.6068 7.625 16.5778 8.63398 16.5778 9.875V16.625C16.5778 17.866 15.6068 18.875 14.4124 18.875H3.58534C2.39097 18.875 1.41992 17.866 1.41992 16.625V9.875C1.41992 8.63398 2.39097 7.625 3.58534 7.625H4.12669Z" fill="#0B0C0C"/></svg></a>.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h5> Supply market analysis and early engagement </h5>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>Early market engagement can lead to increased competition, promote innovation and improve value for money for contracts. Commercial specialists should ensure that potential suppliers have sufficient time to appropriately influence, understand and prepare to make an offer against the contract requirements when advertised (except in the case of a catalogue procurement) and the outcomes that are expected to be delivered.</p>
<p>A commercial specialist should assess the business need by conducting supply market analysis in order to recommend the most appropriate market engagement approach. Outcomes from the market engagement should be used to shape the business need, define the contract requirements and develop the commercial options.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h5> Analysis of commercial options</h5>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>Identifying and analysing commercial options enables effective appraisal and selection of the optimum commercial approach to deliver the intended outcome. Justification for choosing a particular commercial option should be documented. This should be done through cross-functional analysis and the timely production of commercial cases. Options should be assessed following the requirements of the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/government-analysis-functional-standard--2" class="link" ><em>Government Functional Standard for Analysis</em></a>.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h5> Setting criteria for selecting suppliers</h5>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>The criteria for selecting suppliers and offer evaluation method should be established before inviting offers from the supply market. Offer evaluation criteria should enable differentiation between supplier offers and should consider both priced and unpriced elements to identify the most economically advantageous offer.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.3.4                                                     Procure the goods, works or services </h4>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h5> Overview</h5>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>Procuring services and goods involves:</p>
<ul>
<li>agreeing the route to market and procurement procedure</li>
<li>selecting form of contracts</li>
<li>preparing the draft contract</li>
<li>inviting offers</li>
<li>evaluation of offers and selection of suppliers</li>
<li>contract award</li>
</ul>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h5> Agreeing the route to market and procurement procedure</h5>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>The appropriate route to market is informed by the selected commercial approach and the associated complexity and risks. Project delivery teams should draw on the expertise of commercial specialists as appropriate to agree the route to market for non-transactional contracts. Additional advice might be needed from the chief commercial officer of the organisation for the most complex of contracts.</p>
<p>The selected route to market should be justified and aligned to the selected commercial option while complying with commercial policy and regulations and ensuring opportunities are accessible.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h5> Selecting a form of contract</h5>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>A form of contract should be selected before inviting offers from the market. Model forms of contract should be used except when otherwise justified to facilitate more efficient sourcing and contract management. The <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/model-services-contract" class="link" ><em>Model services contract</em></a> should be used as a reference for which terms and conditions should be used for major services contracts. It is intended for use by commercial specialists and lawyers to reduce administration, legal costs and negotiation time.</p>
<p>Proportionate key performance indicators should be refined, defined and included in contracts. These indicators should be developed in consultation with relevant stakeholders and be published in line with policy.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h5> Preparing the draft contract</h5>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>A draft contract and supporting tender documentation should be prepared using the chosen form of contract. Contracts can be output or outcome based and should be designed to promote proactive commercial assurance through its terms and conditions.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h5> Inviting or identifying offers</h5>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>Suppliers should be invited to submit documented offers to deliver the requirement or, where a procurement involves using a pre-existing framework, catalogue or dynamic purchasing system, supplier offers should be identified. This should be done in accordance with the commercial governance and management framework, the organisation’s processes and controls and in compliance with regulations.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h5> Evaluation of offers and selection of suppliers</h5>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>Effective supplier selection and evaluation of offers ensures the appropriate supplier is chosen to undertake the work to deliver the required outcomes and that value for money is achieved.</p>
<p>Proportionate due diligence should be carried out on the selected supplier before recommending a contract award. The evaluation of supplier proposals should be carried out using the criteria defined. Evaluations should be conducted with cross-functional support with evaluators having no conflicts of interest that could prejudice the activity and award.</p>
<p>Contract award recommendations should be justified and approved. Where the contract is to develop or deliver the main solution for the work, this is normally combined with approval of the full business case.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h5> Contract award</h5>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>Finalised contracts should reflect the negotiations with the prospective supplier and be signed by authorised representatives from the contracting party, after the required ‘standstill’ period. Negotiations should include documenting each contracting party’s liabilities and obligations and any transition responsibilities.</p>
<p>The unsuccessful bidder(s) should be notified, and details of the awarded contract should be published on the relevant procurement portals.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.3.5                                                     Mobilise for delivery</h4>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>Mobilisation begins delivery against the contract. Arrangements should establish the use of a contract management plan which defines the roles and responsibilities of each party and should be periodically reviewed. Any obligations under <em><a href="https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2006/246/contents" class="link" title="The Transfer of Undertakings (Protection of Employment) Regulations 2006 (TUPE)">The Transfer of Undertakings (Protection of Employment) Regulations 2006 (TUPE)</a></em> in respect of employee transfers must be fulfilled as soon as the contract takes effect.</p>
<p>The support required from commercial specialists should be proportionate to the complexity and risks of the contract, with the simplest and lowest cost of contracts potentially needing no specialist support.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.3.6                                                     Plan how the contract is managed</h4>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>A contract management plan should be produced by the contract manager and should be approved by the senior business owner which, in the case of programmes and projects, is likely to be the senior responsible owner and for portfolios the portfolio director.</p>
<p>The contract management plan should include aspects such as:</p>
<ul>
<li>definition of the contract management team, including roles and responsibilities</li>
<li>contract risk management approach and the relationship with the portfolio, programme or project risk management</li>
<li>performance indicators</li>
<li>formal and informal communications channels</li>
<li>dispute resolution provisions, including informal and formal resolution, arbitration and any step-in rights</li>
<li>contingency options</li>
<li>the plan for exit or transition</li>
<li>the plan for re-procurement or contract extension if applicable</li>
<li>the processes and tools required to support contract administration, monitor delivery and manage performance</li>
</ul>
<p>The budget and processes for committing and monitoring contract spend should be established (see <a href="https://projectdelivery.gov.uk/teal-book/home/part-e-planning-and-control/chapter-29-finance/" class="link" title="Chapter 29: Finance">Chapter 29: Finance</a>).</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.3.7                                                     Manage delivery and supplier performance</h4>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>The delivery of goods, works and services should be managed proportionately to the complexity, value and risk of the contract. Supplier performance should be monitored to ensure that intended outputs are delivered to contractual milestones and that outcomes and benefits from contracts are realised.</p>
<p>The contract manager should ensure that the necessary resources, processes and systems are in place that enables:</p>
<ul>
<li>the supplier to be instructed</li>
<li>delivery against contractual obligations, including key performance indicators and milestones, to be tracked</li>
<li>performance and benefits to be monitored and quality to be assured</li>
<li>continuous improvement</li>
<li>supplier invoices to be verified and validated, and then prompt payments made, including through the supply chain</li>
<li>opportunities for innovation to be identified</li>
<li>contract disputes to be managed</li>
</ul>
<p>The contract manager should regularly report contract performance to the portfolio, programme or project manager and other relevant stakeholders, in support of monitoring the effective application of the contract management plan and the performance of the supplier.</p>
<p>Where performance does not or is unlikely to meet the requirements of the contract, preventative or corrective actions should be taken. These actions should be within the terms of the contract and should be aimed as remediating the situation. Examples include issuing a formal notice or issuing a notice for a performance improvement plan. Where performance does not improve, or in the event of serious or persistent breach of contract, specialist commercial advice, and if necessary legal advice, should be sought. Contract performance and any performance management action taken should be rigorously documented, ensuring that both client and supplier obligations are met at all times.</p>
<p>Periodically, through the life of the contract, the senior responsible owner, supported by the contract manager and commercial specialists, should review the contract and its arrangements. The aim of such reviews is to ensure that the contract accurately reflects the parties’ relationship, current risks, market conditions and that the contract continues to deliver the business needs and provides value for money.</p>
<p>Over the life of the contract, changes may be identified that need to be managed. All contract changes should be justified and controlled to ensure that the requirements continue to meet the business needs and align to the organisation’s financial processes. Contract change control should be fully integrated and aligned to the change control processes for the portfolio, programme or project (see <a href="https://projectdelivery.gov.uk/teal-book/home/part-e-planning-and-control/chapter-22-change-control/" class="link" title="Chapter 22: Change control">Chapter 22: Change control</a>).</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.3.8                                                     Provide advice and support</h4>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>During the life of the contract, the advice and support of commercial specialists might be needed. Advice and support can be provided on a range of topics and should be sought on aspects such as:</p>
<ul>
<li>performance issues and the implementing of preventative or corrective actions</li>
<li>benchmarking prices against the market and other public sector organisations</li>
<li>contractual disputes</li>
<li>contractual risk management and techniques, such as stress testing, scenario planning and contract contingency plans</li>
</ul>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.3.9                                                     Contract transition and exit</h4>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>Contract transition ensures that handover is conducted smoothly with no unplanned interruption to service and happens in situations such as:</p>
<ul>
<li>where a programme or project is coming to an end, and managing the delivery of the service needs to transition from the programme or project team to an operational team</li>
<li>where the delivery of the service is transitioning from one supplier to another</li>
</ul>
<p>A transition plan should be established which defines the goals, responsibilities and activities of the transition. The plan should follow the guidance in <a href="https://projectdelivery.gov.uk/teal-book/home/part-f-solution-delivery/chapter-36-transition-into-use/" class="link" title="Chapter 36: Transition into use">Chapter 36: Transition into use</a> and include:</p>
<ul>
<li>knowledge asset and data handover</li>
<li>supplier staff transition</li>
<li>contingency plans</li>
</ul>
<p>Commercial knowledge assets can include intellectual property, research, data, expertise and other intellectual resources that have been developed by third-party suppliers when delivering a contract.</p>
<p>Contracts may be exited either when completed or when terminated early and can happen during the life cycle of a programme or project, or during their closure. Formal notice is usually required and should be reflected in planning. An exit plan may be separate or can be included in the contract management plan and should include:</p>
<ul>
<li>clear outline of activities, milestones and required resources</li>
<li>roles, responsibilities and accountabilities</li>
<li>any residual obligations in respect of supplier employees under the <em><a href="https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2006/246/contents" class="link" title="The Transfer of Undertakings (Protection of Employment) Regulations 2006">The Transfer of Undertakings (Protection of Employment) Regulations 2006</a></em></li>
<li>key interfaces and dependencies</li>
<li>asset registers and transfers</li>
</ul>
<p>Early termination of a contract should be a last resort, only enacted after other provisions for the delivery of the contract, including remedies, have been exhausted. When early termination is proposed, the cost and impact of the termination should be considered, including the likelihood and implications of any legal dispute, and specialist commercial and legal advice should be sought.</p>
<p>On contract closure, information systems should be updated, any staff and facilities reassigned and the contract documentation archived.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>

                                        
                                            <div class="mt-3  single-section">
                                                <div class="single-heading">
                                                    <h4>                                                    25.6.3.10                                                     Close procurement and contract management framework</h4>
                                                </div>
                                                                                                <div class="single-content mt-1">
                                                    <p>In a programme or project, following completion of the work, commercial management arrangements are brought to a close. In a portfolio, commercial management arrangements normally continue unless the portfolio is fully concluded and wound up, or substantially reset.</p>
<p>In some programmes or projects, commercial data, reporting and accounting arrangements are handed over to support commercial management as part of operations, particularly where there are ongoing contracts or follow up activities following programme or project close, or where the work moves into a sustainment model (whereby future development is carried out on an iterative basis as part of business as usual operations).</p>
<p>The effectiveness of commercial management should be evaluated as part of closing the work. Commercial management information should be archived in accordance with the sponsoring organisation’s information and data retention policies <span style="font-weight: 400;"> (see</span> <a href="https://projectdelivery.gov.uk/teal-book/the-teal-book/part-e-planning-and-control/chapter-24-information-and-data-management/" class="link" title="Chapter 24: Information and data management">Chapter 24: Information and data management</a>). The procurement and contract management framework should then be closed.</p>
                                                </div>
                                                 
                                            </div>
